“Some standing here” was fulfilled at the transfiguration, six days later.

“All Israel will be saved”: in this way
Does Romans 11:26 promise a future national conversion of ethnic Israel, with a rebuilt temple and a throne in Jerusalem, or something Paul was already seeing?
Start where Paul starts
Romans 11 answers a question raised in chapter 9: has God's word failed, now that most of Israel has rejected the Messiah?
Paul defines Israel
Not everyone descended from Israel is Israel. The children of the promise, not simply the children of the flesh, are counted as Abraham's offspring.
A remnant, now
Isaiah foresaw that only a remnant would be saved. Like the 7,000 of Elijah's day, there was a remnant chosen by grace in Paul's own time.
Hardening opens the door
Part of Israel was hardened so the Gentiles could come in. Believing Gentiles are grafted into the same olive tree, not a second one.
The Greek houtōs means “so” or “in this manner”, not “after that”. In this way, by the remnant plus the grafted-in Gentiles, all Israel is saved.
Galatians agrees
The promise went to one Seed, Christ. All who belong to Christ, Jew or Greek, are Abraham's offspring and heirs; Paul blesses “the Israel of God”.

Many readers, including some who reject dispensationalism, take “all Israel” in 11:26 as ethnic Israel, because “Israel” in 11:25 plainly means the hardened nation. They expect a large turning of Jewish people to Christ before the end, and point to “their full inclusion” (11:12) and “life from the dead” (11:15).

Paul's own definition, the remnant he could already see, and the meaning of “in this way” point to one people of God in Christ. Nothing in the chapter requires a rebuilt temple, sacrifices or a throne in Jerusalem.

A future turning of many Jewish people to Christ is held by many postmillennial and Reformed teachers too; it fits a growing kingdom. The point here is that Romans 11 offers no separate plan apart from the church. It is never a reason for hostility to Jewish people.
“All things written” and a finished work
Jesus called AD 70 the days of vengeance, when all that was written would be fulfilled. What does that leave for a third temple and a future earthly millennium?
The bookends of Revelation
The book opens and closes with the same time words: these things must soon take place, the time is near, I am coming soon.
The days of vengeance
Speaking of Jerusalem surrounded by armies, Jesus says these are the days of vengeance, so that all that is written may be fulfilled.
The Song of Moses
Moses foretold Israel's latter end (Hebrew acharit) and called them a perverse generation with no faith. Jesus and Peter use the same words for their own generation.
Abel to Zechariah
Jesus said all the righteous blood shed on earth would come upon that generation, and that all these things would come upon it.
The thousand is a symbol
Revelation was “signified”. God owns the cattle on a thousand hills and keeps covenant for a thousand generations: a thousand means fullness, not a count.
No way back to shadows
The old covenant was “ready to vanish”. Going back to animal sacrifice after the cross would treat Christ's once-for-all offering as insufficient.
Reigning now
Christ is already seated on David's throne at the Father's right hand. Believers are not in a waiting room but share in a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

Futurists answer that Luke 21:22 means all that was written about Jerusalem's judgement, not every prophecy; that “soon” can mean suddenly, or soon in God's reckoning (2 Peter 3:8); and that Ezekiel 40-48 describes a real temple still to be built.
Taken at their word, the time texts place the judgement of the old covenant order in the first century. A rebuilt temple with renewed sacrifices has no place after the finished work of Christ.

Partial preterists usually read “all things written” as all that was written about Jerusalem's judgement, and see the thousand years as the whole present reign of Christ, still going on, not a span ending in AD 70. Scripture still promises Christ's bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgement (Acts 1:11; 1 Corinthians 15:23-28). Saying all prophecy is fulfilled denies these, and the creeds reject it.
“Some standing here”: Matthew 16:27-28
Jesus said some of those standing with him would not die before they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom. Which event fits?
A coming about to happen
The Greek mellō means “about to”. Jesus speaks of a coming that is near, not twenty centuries away.
Five details to match
He comes in his Father's glory, with his angels, repays each person for what they have done, and some, not all, of those present are still alive to see it.
The transfiguration?
It came six days later, while all were alive. No angels came and no one was judged; Jesus himself called it a vision.
Pentecost?
It too came while nearly all were alive, and it was a gift of the Spirit, not a coming to repay each person for their deeds.

Many readers, including some who hold the fulfilled reading of Matthew 24, link the saying to the transfiguration, which follows at once in all three Gospels (Mark 9:1-8; Luke 9:27-36), and note that Peter later calls it a sight of Christ's power and coming (2 Peter 1:16-18).
Only an event decades later, which some but not all would live to see, fits every detail. AD 70 does; the transfiguration and Pentecost do not.

Answer gently: “I know how you feel; I once felt the same; here is what I found.” Many link the transfiguration to the coming as a preview of it rather than the event itself. Christ's final bodily return remains a future hope in every orthodox reading.
